title: How can young people contribute to their communities?
essentialQuestion: How can one person help solve a problem or strengthen a community?
learningGoal: Plan a small, safe and realistic way to help a community, using evidence and working with others.

warmUp.question: Which of these would help a learning centre the most?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: Which idea uses evidence, works with others and keeps people safe?

cards.title: Learners' ideas after seeing litter at the bus stop outside Hillside Learning Centre

cases.name: Idea 1
cases.body: Post one angry message online about the mess.

cases.name: Idea 2
cases.body: With a teacher, ask people who use the bus stop what is missing, such as a bin or a sign. Then ask the centre manager for permission to hold a one-hour clean-up, with gloves, bags and a plan for taking the rubbish away.

cases.name: Idea 3
cases.body: Write a short, polite letter to the centre manager. Include what bus users said, a photo of the litter with no people in it, and one suggestion, such as a new bin.

cards.title: Other everyday ways to help
items: Translating for a new learner who is still learning English
Keeping a shared room clean and tidy
Joining or starting a club, such as a chess, art or football club
Teaching a friend a skill, like drawing or a game

sections.heading: Small actions can help a community
sections.text: To contribute means to give your time, skills or help to make something better. Contributing does not have to mean a big campaign, because everyday actions matter too. A learner can read with a younger child, translate for someone who is new, keep a shared room clean or join a club. These actions help people learn, feel welcome and share the work of a community. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child says that children have the right to give their views on things that affect them. It also says that children can join or set up groups and meet with others.
sections.simpler: To contribute is to give your time or help to make things better. You do not need to do something big. Small acts help a community too. You can read with a young child. You can translate for a new learner. You can clean a room you share. You can join a club. The United Nations has a list of rights for children. It says children can give their views. It also says they can join groups.

sections.heading: Start with evidence and work together
sections.text: Learners at Hillside Learning Centre noticed litter near the bus stop outside. They had three ideas. Idea 1, an angry post online, might upset people and would not fix the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask people who use the bus stop what is missing. People who are affected by a problem are called stakeholders. Here, the stakeholders include bus users, the learners and the centre manager. Idea 3 turns the evidence into a short, polite letter to the manager with one clear suggestion, such as a new bin. Working with others makes a plan fairer and more likely to succeed.
sections.simpler: Some learners saw litter near a bus stop. They had three ideas. Idea 1 was an angry post. It would not fix the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask bus users what is missing. Stakeholders are people who are affected by a problem. Bus users are stakeholders. So is the centre manager. Idea 3 is a short, polite letter to the manager. It asks for a new bin.

sections.heading: Stay safe and look back
sections.text: Good contributions are safe. Before a clean-up, the learners talk to a teacher and get permission from the centre manager. They plan to use gloves and bags, and they arrange for the rubbish to be taken away. If they take a photo of the litter, it should not show anyone's face or private information. You never need to speak in public, post online or take risks to contribute. After acting, look back and ask: What changed? Who was included? What would we do differently next time? Even a small change, like a cleaner bus stop, can make a difference.
sections.simpler: Helping must be safe. First, the learners talk to a teacher. The centre manager gives permission. They use gloves and bags. They plan where the rubbish goes. A photo must not show faces. You do not need to speak in public or post online. After you help, look back. What changed? Who was included? What can be better next time?

glossary.definition: To give your time, skills or help to make something better.
glossary.example: Reading with a younger child is one way to contribute.

glossary.definition: A group of people who live, learn or work near each other.
glossary.example: The learners and staff at Hillside Learning Centre are a community.

glossary.definition: Facts that show what is really happening.
glossary.example: What bus users say about the missing bin is evidence.

glossary.definition: A person or group that a problem or plan affects.
glossary.example: Bus users and the centre manager are stakeholders.

glossary.definition: When the person in charge says yes, you may do something.
glossary.example: The learners get permission from the centre manager before the clean-up.

checks.question: Which idea starts by asking people and working together?

options.text: Idea 1, posting one angry message online
options.feedback: Not quite. An angry post does not ask anyone for information. Look for the idea that starts with evidence.

options.text: Idea 2, asking bus users what is missing
options.feedback: Yes. Idea 2 starts by asking the stakeholders. That gives the learners evidence to plan with.

options.text: Waiting for someone else to clean it up
options.feedback: Not quite. Waiting does not help or ask anyone. Look for the idea that starts with evidence.

checks.question: Why should the learners get permission before a clean-up?

options.text: To keep everyone safe and make a plan
options.feedback: Yes. With permission, an adult knows the plan, and the clean-up can be safe and well organised.

options.text: To make sure that nobody else can help
options.feedback: Not quite. Permission helps people take part safely. Read the section about staying safe again.

options.text: Because a clean-up is against the rules
options.feedback: Not quite. A clean-up is not against the rules. Permission makes sure it is safe and planned.

checks.question: Which stakeholder should the learners talk to first? Why?
checks.placeholder: They should talk to ___ first, because ___.

write.prompt: Make a small plan for the bus-stop litter or another small problem at a learning centre. Say your goal, how you will get evidence, who you will ask and one way to stay safe.
selfCheck: I chose a small, realistic goal.
I included one safety or permission step.
I planned how to check what changed.
write.example: Our goal is to make the bus stop outside our centre cleaner. First, we will find out what is missing. With our teacher, we will ask five bus users. We will ask our teacher and the centre manager for permission to hold a one-hour clean-up. To stay safe, we will wear gloves, work in pairs and put the rubbish in bags for the centre to take away. We will not take photos of people. Afterwards, we will check the bus stop again and ask users if they see a change.

speak.partnerTask: Practise a short, polite request to the centre manager about the bus stop. Your partner plays the manager and asks one question.
speak.independentTask: Explain your action plan in 30 seconds, or write it as three short steps.

watch.title: Young people have a message for world leaders
watch.why: It shows young people sharing their ideas with the people who make decisions.
watch.beforeQuestion: What makes a message to people in charge useful?
watch.afterQuestion: What help do young people need so that adults listen to their ideas?
watch.summary: In this UNICEF video, young people share messages for world leaders. They talk about how climate change affects their lives and the places where they live. They ask leaders to listen to young people and to act. The video shows that young people have good ideas about problems that affect them. But ideas need to reach the right people. For this to work, young people need facts, help from adults and a real chance to change what happens. You do not have to speak to world leaders to make a difference. You can also help in small, safe ways, like reading with a younger child or keeping a shared space clean.
keyPoints: Young people have useful ideas about problems that affect them.
Young people need information, support and a real chance to be heard.
You can also contribute in small, safe, everyday ways.
watch.contentNote: Young people talk about climate impacts. Preview the video first. Learners may stop at any time, and no public activism is expected.

reflect.completionMessage: You finished Lesson 24. You planned a small, safe way to help a community, and you finished the whole course.

visual.description: A calm street scene outside Hillside Learning Centre. Four learners of different ages, with a teacher, wear gloves and put litter into bags near a bus stop. One learner holds a clipboard and talks with a bus user sitting on the bench. The centre manager stands at the centre's door, smiling and giving a thumbs-up. A new bin with a small sign stands beside the bus stop. Bright daytime, no traffic danger.
visual.alt: Learners and a teacher wearing gloves clean up litter at a bus stop outside their learning centre. One learner asks a bus user questions while the centre manager watches and approves.

sources.label: UNICEF: Children's version of the Convention on the Rights of the Child
UNICEF video: Young people have a message for world leaders

educatorNotes: Keep every action inside or next to the learning centre, with the centre's permission and an adult involved. Do not ask learners to contact authorities, join protests or post online. This matters especially for learners whose legal status is uncertain.
Remind learners not to photograph people or share anyone's private details, including their own.
The video includes young people talking about climate impacts. Preview it; learners may stop at any time, and no activism is expected. If the topic is upsetting, use the written summary instead.

A partner can swap the bus stop for a shared space learners know, such as the centre's yard, a shared kitchen or a playground, and adapt the 'everyday ways to help' list to activities that exist at the centre.
changes: Kept the fictional bus-stop litter scenario but placed it outside Hillside Learning Centre, so the people in charge are the centre manager and a teacher, not outside authorities.
Added a second evidence card of everyday ways to help (reading with a younger child, translating, cleaning a shared room, joining a club) and made these the focus of the first section.
Removed 'civic action' and 'accountability' from the glossary and made the glossary five words used in both versions of the text; the old third section had no glossary words at all.
Added a short, accurate reference to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (the right to give views and to join groups).
Rewrote the simpler English so it is much simpler. It was harder than the main text before.
Made the self-check a list of three 'I...' statements and changed the planning boxes to the standard set.
Moved the video content warning into watch.contentNote, rewrote the summary so it stands alone, and fixed the completion message (the course name is now in the text, not the first sentence).
